children: By Gunjan Banerji
Americans are piling into stocks — even in the face of a brutal AI downturn.

A torrent of money has flooded into exchange-traded and mutual funds tracking U.S. stocks, at a pace with little precedent in recent history. These funds have attracted more than $450 billion in fresh cash this year, on track for a record, according to EPFR data analyzed by Deutsche Bank.

The steady stream of investment has continued even as the AI trade unraveled over the past month, a dizzying stretch of swings impacted by everything from the U.S. midterm elections to the boardroom-and-espionage drama at Nvidia. But through it all, more than $141 billion has flowed into U.S. equity funds this month, through Nov. 18 — even as the S&P 500 dropped 3.4%.
"The selloff has been met with huge inflows into U.S. equity funds," said Parag Thatte, an equity strategist at Deutsche Bank.

This insatiable appetite during this bull market, which turned four years old in October, has left many American households more exposed to stocks — and its ups and downs — than ever before. U.S. stocks recently comprised more than 40% of U.S. households' total financial assets, a record going back to the 1950s, according to Ed Clissold, chief U.S. strategist at Ned Davis Research.
U.S. stock funds added more new money than they lost for 13 consecutive months through September, the longest streak in EPFR data going back to 2000.

These inflows include investments on autopilot that more Americans make through retirement plans such as 401(k) accounts, as well as discretionary purchases. Some investors are still "buying the dip" — stepping in when their favorite stocks take a hit.
That commitment to buying stocks means Americans' wealth is also tied to the artificial-intelligence trade. AI stocks powered the market's gains for three years, before plunging in recent weeks.

Three years of double-digit returns, and even bigger gains from AI stocks, led many everyday investors to double down. Some Gen Z Americans have ditched homeownership, diverting would-be down payments to the stock market instead. Baby boomers, who have long been advised to take chips off the table, increasingly hold more of their portfolios in stocks. Many even borrowed to amplify their exposure to stocks this year.

In the mid-1980s, when Ronald Reagan was president, fewer than 30% of households held stocks, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. By the early 2000s, more than half of them did. Recently, that figure hovered around 56%, according to the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances.

As Americans' finances grow more intertwined with the stock market, a prolonged selloff could have far-reaching effects. With the S&P 500 down 6.7% from its October record, many investors are logging on to their retirement accounts and seeing red.

Many investors have grown accustomed to lightning-fast reversals after downturns, such as those during the 2020 market crash during the Covid-19 pandemic and after "Liberation Day" last year, when President Trump's sweeping tariffs triggered a brief rout.

This recent stretch of AI-fueled volatility has dragged on for weeks and has been marked by headspinning swings that are tough for even seasoned investors to navigate. U.S. stocks recently recorded one of their worst weeks since the March 2020 crash. Many AI-related shares have fallen more than 40% from highs. The S&P 500, a real-time barometer of wealth for many of these investors, came close to wiping out its gains for the year.
Americans who are all in on the stock market, and continue to buy during big declines, are facing one of their biggest tests yet.
Following Friday's 2.3% move higher, the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite has tumbled 13% from its record hit in early October and remains in correction territory.

Strong flows into funds have been closely correlated with a stretch of strong corporate earnings reports. If investors start to doubt corporate America's ability to keep churning out profits, they might stop buying, Deutsche Bank's Thatte said.

Many of the inflows have been concentrated in exchange-traded funds, which have drawn more than $880 billion this year, a record high, according to State Street Investment Management. Mutual funds have recorded outflows.

What these investors do could have big implications for the markets. U.S. households are the largest holders of U.S. stocks, according to Goldman Sachs. And in the coming weeks, individual investors' confidence in a rebound may be the only thing standing in the way of a major downturn.

"Following a performance bloodbath and severe derisking by hedge funds during October, the support from retail investors is essential to stabilize the AI trade in November," JPMorgan's Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou wrote in a note to clients earlier this month.

Economists at Capital Economics said recently that the selloff could quickly weigh on consumer spending. From February to April 2025, a drop in the S&P 500 rapidly led to a decline in consumption, they said. The drop came as Trump's trade war ramped up, driving fears about a recession.
"There's a feedback loop," said Ed Yardeni, founder of Yardeni Research, on the relationship between stocks and consumer spending.
